speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. subtopic: PROPOSED TRANS-ALASKA PIPELINE SYSTEM-CONSULTATIONS WITH UNITED STATES-NORTHERN TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can certainly answer the second part of the question. Obviously no decision has been made since the hearings of the committee that has been established to examine into the ecology and the economics of this pipeline; the matter is still under way.

subtopic: PROPOSED TRANS-ALASKA PIPELINE SYSTEM-CONSULTATIONS WITH UNITED STATES-NORTHERN TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, arising out of statements made on a two-hour television program last night by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development indicating that they are taking a rather casual attitude to the transportation of northern oil. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED TRANS-ALASKA PIPELINE SYSTEM-CONSULTATIONS WITH UNITED STATES-NORTHERN TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a number of answers were given yesterday to these questions and there is really very little I can add to what was said on that occasion. I believe it is most important that a decision about the building of the trans-Alaska pipeline system be made in light of the great risks and dangers that exist to the Pacific coast. This is a matter of supreme importance not only to the people of Canada but to the people of the United States. From our point of view, a decision adverse to the building of that pipeline would leave us in the position of looking at the problems of alternative routes free of any prejudice.

subtopic: PROPOSED TRANS-ALASKA PIPELINE SYSTEM-CONSULTATIONS WITH UNITED STATES-NORTHERN TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Can the minister give any indication as to when the government intends to make a decision on its stand in connection with the transportation of oil?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED TRANS-ALASKA PIPELINE SYSTEM-CONSULTATIONS WITH UNITED STATES-NORTHERN TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what we are talking about now is the transportation of Alaska oil. The United States has the problem of finding some safe and economic way of transporting this oil from the state of Alaska to other states of the union. The question as to which is the better route is, first of all, one to be considered in the United States. I have expressed the view of the Canadian government that it would be very risky to transport that oil down the Pacific coast to Bellingham. I have urged the people of Canada and the United States to express their views quite clearly on that question so that a decision can be made with a clear understanding of the great risks that are involved. That is the question at the moment. The question of whether United States companies want to apply to transport their oil through Canada is a separate question. They have not yet applied.

maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-HOUSE DEBATE BEFORE FINAL DECISION

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Finance arising out of press reports from Washington. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF EXEMPTION FROM UNITED STATES INTEREST EQUALIZATION TAX-CANADIAN U.S. DOLLAR RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I understand the situation, the President of the United States has requested an extension of the interest equalization tax, including a continuation of the exemption for Canada. I believe this has been approved by the house committee and is presently before the senate committee in the United States and will be considered by it. I wish to be believed, Mr. Speaker. We do not even want the bill to reach the stage of the committee of the House.
That is why we object right from second reading, not for the sole purpose of uselessly extending the debate but to let the people of Canada know not only where their taxes go but also how they are taxed.
Here, Mr. Speaker, I call the attention of the House quite especially on a remark, unkind to say the least, made last night by the Acting Speaker while he probably commented on my speech.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make this the subject of a question of privilege but in order not to delay the proceedings of the House, I thought it would be better to call your attention on that during my speech because I knew that I would have the floor as soon as the debate resumes.

I must say that this House today reminds me of my family motto, "Sat seto si sat bene"-which roughly translated means "let us proceed slowly, but surely".

I would not want to be forced to entertain a regrettable opinion contrary to the one I have always had regarding the Chair. When this so-called social development surtax was applied, the government promised it would be in effect for only two years, just long enough to fight inflation, as we were told then. And now a continuation of its application is being sought for another year, that is until 1972.
Just for another year, and another year, and another year. The population just have to swallow those increasing taxes, mouthful after mouthful. We know the old party line and what an Indian would so aptly call their forked tongue.
The most striking demonstration of this fraud was given us during the Second World War. As everyone remembers, the government seized this golden opportunity to borrow from the provinces three of their fields of taxation, thus robbing them of all revenues, of course, formally promising to return it all at the end of the war.
The Liberal government, like the one we now have, committed a breach of trust against the provinces. More than 30 years have elapsed since that momentous promise, and the provinces are still waiting for the government to return their tax fields. Not only that, but they continue repeating every five years what is being asked of us today, an extension designed to bring the false promises, making the provinces even more dependent on the federal government.
What is most alarming and most unexplainable, is the practically approving silence of the Progressive Conservatives and of members of the New Democratic Party. That is why I hope they will take the floor today and explain their attitude. When it comes to levying a new tax or extending its application, I wonder what keeps them in their seats. They probably think about the government. They have been told so many times that there were only two ways in which to govern a country, that is to say through taxes and loans, that they feel powerless in front of this myth, entirely invented by financiers in order to get us under better control.
As for us, Creditistes, we do know that this should be the last recourse for a sound and logical government. Consequently, we understand the existence of taxes and loans for a poor country like India; but we cannot do so for a rich one like Canada. There is no accounting for it, unless it should be a patent robbery of our heritage, with the complicity of the government.
Indeed, we can compare a country to a family farm, to simplify things. If the family farm yields fair profits, its owner and the whole family take advantage of it, provided that a thief should not find its way inside and take off with the whole production. Canada is the third most productive country in the world and it has the lowest population in relation to its size. Its owners which should be the people of Canada, must benefit from those resources. But it happens that a burglar, that is high finance, gains entry into the country and takes over the best sources of income. The people must therefore resort to taxes and loans to carry on their administration. That results in deprivation for our people, indebtedness, unemployment, and all its consequences.
We pay $2 billion per year for interest alone on a fictional national debt because the Bank of Canada has never fulfilled its function. We pay social development taxes, unemployment taxes, social insurance taxes, national administration taxes, and we continue to let ourselves be robbed by a "supergovernment", which is antisocial and which will bring about our social and economic ruin.
I wonder if our good old parties will finally realize the monstrous character of our false financial system, which allows those who control the economy to loan more and more at unlimited rates, as the government has removed cealings in the last few years, thus authorizing colossal interest rates affecting mostly low-income people. In fact, I had discussions with important financial institutions in order to find out the reason for the difference in rates, as each of these companies has a separate rate scale. I was told that the greater the risk, the higher the interest rate, which means that the borrower who is least able to pay has to be charged the highest interest rate. And I was stupefied to see that the low-income worker unable to supply much collateral had to pay 10, 15 or 20 per cent more than people highly rated by big financiers.

and for all those taxes which take away the required purchasing power from our Canadian families?
The government should refrain from taxing the necessities of life and to this end, it should raise the tax exemption for married people to $6,000 and for single persons to $3,500. It should abolish the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, to enable low income families to own their home too. In addition, it should not extend its temporary taxes.
I ask the government and the other opposition parties to put a stop to this constant extension from year to year of a tax which is permanent, even if it is referred to as being temporary.
At this condition only will we give the population justice and this is the only way to allow the average Canadian to participate also in the economic recovery so desired by the government by investing in our Canadian companies instead of having to sell them to Americans because the people are too much in debt.
There is evidence that we hold the world record for indebtedness for the simple reason that our financial system is based upon indebtedness and our so-called money is debt money. The more we develop, the more debts we create and as evidence of this, I shall quote an article published in La Presse on June 29, 1969 under the title: "Les Canadiens sont deux fois plus endettes qu'en 1960". The same thing could be said for each year. Here is a part of that article:
Some $9,200,000,000. That is the total indebtedness of Canadians as at the end of 1968, excluding mortgages.
It is an increase of almost $700,000,000 over the preceding year and double that of 1960.
Neither bankers, nor finance companies, nor economists can yet see a limit to the Canadian credit upsurge. They do not even discern any sign of it levelling off.
Far from it, Mr. Speaker.
I was reading in a financial publication yesterday that banks had made unprecedented profits in 1970. I think this success is due to the protection the government has extended to them through removal of the ceiling on interest rates. In fact, the money these banks are lending is altogether created since they are entitled to lend 14 times the equivalent of their actual assets at interest rates of 10 or 11 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, is it any wonder that ours is the most indebted people in the world?
Can the economy be stimulated through new taxes slapped on the back of the workers? Or is it feared that the worker, unless he is saturated with taxes as he is today, might yet lift his head to pit himself against the giants of Canadian and American finance?
Can the government at least give us a logical reason for those taxes that the people cannot digest any longer? But no! The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), in all his arrogance, so ordained, and the people must pay. The government, strong in its absolute parliamentary majority, blinded by its victories over the people, cannot feel the tremors under its feet.

In olden days, serfs where whipped or men were chained. Today, they are squeezed under the steam-roller of taxes and surtaxes. It is more sophisticated, but all the more cruel because human beings are thus very often led to commit suicide.
Mr. Speaker, I need not repeat that we are against that extension, that we no longer want those ridiculous extensions, and we insist that the government simply withdraw this bill, and not refer it to the standing committee for consideration. Now what is there to consider in this bill? Nothing at all. It is at most a formality which will allow this bill to be enacted.
Yesterday, I met a member from the official opposition who told me: We are not going to speak on second reading, we are going to let the bill go to committee and are going to speak on third reading. Well, it will be too late. It is being discussed on second reading as a joke, because there is absolutely nothing to discuss in it.
And what shall we do on third reading? As always, the government will call the vote and the bill will be passed and the people will once again be the victims.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be party to these taxes and surtaxes, and I ask the government to keep for once, if it never did, its promise and to drop this legislation which was to stay in effect for only two years. Let us be assured that the people, the workers-because this legislation again affects only the average worker-have had enough of paying the surtax for two years and will not allow it to be extended.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-225 purports to extend for another year the 3 p. 100 temporary surtax imposed in 1968.
Ever since then, the government has tabled each year a similar bill, which leads me to believe that they are not acting fairly towards the Canadian taxpayer; this procedure is tantamount to making a permanent tax out of a temporary one.
In my opinion, if matters were dealt with in a like manner by municipal governments, of which I was a member for a part of my life especially at the rural level, no taxpayer would trust the administrators at all.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) brought down his supplementary budget in December last, he clearly stated and I quote:
In order to meet our cash requirements for the coming year, without resorting to excessive borrowing on the market, the government proposes that the 3 per cent surtax on personal and corporate incomes be extended for another year. The receipts from this tax are estimated at $245 million for the 1971 calendar year.
This means that individuals will have $245 million less in purchasing power, as well as corporations, to further develop industries and give employment, if possible, to Canadian workers.

The real thieves should be sought and one should leave alone the poor people who are constantly worried and wonder if they will be able to continue to pay their taxes, their insurance premiums, their school and municipal taxes. I witness such cases every day and every weekend I get more than I can handle. It is my duty to look after them and to raise the matter in order to draw the attention of the government and convince it to do something for those people.
The poor are often called underprivileged. They have been disinherited. They are denied their status of joint heirs to the national wealth we possess in Canada, a right equally shared by all citizens of the country. They should co-inherit the progress that is the main factor of modem production and be entitled to a share of the production resulting from that progress.
If the returns of production are distributed only among financial backers and employees, that means that the share of the underprivileged went to financiers and wage-earners. By taking from these through taxes to assist the underprivileged one does not reinstate these underprivileged in their rights; these allowances leave them with their status of underprivileged and welfare recipients, whereas they should be recognized as joint heirs and joint social capitalists, receiving a social dividend, not as assistance to indigents, but as money due to capitalists. This would be an "operation dignity" ensuring every member of society some degree of economic security, a standard of life proportional to the volume of production, without suppressing the remuneration of those producers who develop the community's capital.
Technical advance would no longer be detrimental if it did away with jobs. On the contrary, the social dividend, ensuring to all a certain standard of living geared to production, and not only to employment, increased mechanization and automation, would free the people and enable them to pursue activities other than the economic function of man, instead of creating new material needs and maintaining work as the sole source of revenue.
Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time that we have asked in this House for a financial reform with a view to freeing the government from the bondage of credit controllers. But the government always refuses to act.
To my knowledge, since 1968, four motions asking for the passage of legislation to guarantee all citizens a minimum income have come before the House. On four occasions, the old-line parties leagued together to vote against those motions which, some day or other, will have to be passed. And the sooner the better. The more there are delays, the worse the problem gets; the more the people are dissatisfied, and the more we witness situations which become more and more nerve-wracking.
The situation is worsening from day to day, as I said earlier. We now have 142,000 unemployed graduates, for whom the state spent considerable sums of money, and whose parents made sacrifices to keep them in school, often by working late at night.

In addition, we are informed that the situation might possibly deteriorate during summer or autumn when waves of new graduates from universities, trade schools and CEGEPs will swell the ranks of educated unemployed. And yet, in December 1970, we had tabled a motion in the House and initiated a debate on the grave subject of the unemployed in the 18-25 age bracket. What did the House do? We played around, as we are doing today, we are not interested in this fundamental matter. This is a small two page bill, but none the less a bill that involves $245 million over the next fiscal year.
Mr. Speaker, where are the people's representatives? I am convinced that the ministers are acting in good faith. But, I wonder about one thing: during the war the administrators were efficient and in spite of numerous material difficulties, lack of manpower and lack of supplies, they succeeded in administering Canada and in allowing every Canadian to pull through. We lived then through a boom period.
These same administrators, once war was over, have become incompetent. When we talk about the unemployment problem, they say: Wait, we have magic formulas on the way. Wait, we will soon have solutions!

Like serious people and sincere Canadians we should take the necessary steps right now to put finance at the service of men so that the government may stand up to credit controllers and give better service to the people. Let us not forget it is time to act. Let us not wait until somebody hits us on the head to make a decision, for as early as 1936, an eminent sociologist said in a lecture he was delivering here at the University of Ottawa: Lastly, if you do not want Communism, take to Social Credit. You will thus have a terrific arm against those enemies.
Mr. Speaker, that is truer in 1971 than in 1936. We have gone a long way since then but not far enough to free ourselves from the financial control over governments that prevents men of good will, not only in government but also in industry, business, external or internal trade, in short in all fields where men of good will give their best, from contributing to Canada's development and helping free Canada from that financial influence.
The more Canada grows, the richer it gets, the more Canadian people are told: Deprive yourselves, live like the poor. And there are more poor people all the time. That is not normal and it is for that reason that I am taking a firm stand today by opposing with all my might the extension of that 3 per cent tax that will make the problem more serious instead of solving it.

Mr. Speaker,
I cannot miss this opportunity to make a few brief remarks on this bill.
We are now considering a bill respecting the 3 per cent surtax, the so-called "social development tax", which had been introduced on a temporary basis only.
When the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) was Minister of Finance, he assured the House when proposing this tax that it would be applied for a limited period of time. This is what is hateful about this tax: it is becoming more and more permanent.
If I remember well, when this measure was introduced by the Minister of Finance I suggested that this tax would become permanent. As the months and the years go by, I think the events are proving me right.
And here what is worse: this social development surtax, a designation that makes it all the more hateful, has made it possible to take about $200 million from the Quebec taxpayers.
It was argued that this was to facilitate the implementation of the medicare legislation and we know that the adherence of Quebec was delayed by one year.
This tax is the reason why they took $200 millions in Quebecers' pockets. The then provincial government, as well as ourselves in the opposition, asked the Minister of Finance to make good to the province of Quebec this amount collected I would not say in an illegal manner, but in an irregular one. But the government ignored our representations and those of the provincial government, and one may wonder whether it was not because the latter was of a political allegiance which failed to please those individuals who rule the country.
At any rate, Mr. Speaker, I say that in imposing this 3 per cent surtax, this government has been far from straightforward, for they stressed the temporary nature of what is now considered to be a permanent surtax. With this kind of action on the government's part, there is deception in the general public as well as a tendency to mistrust the nation's leaders.
Measures and positions like the ones now before us are largely responsible for the lack of confidence in the country's government which prevails within the population.
This legislation is also impeding the economic expansion of our country. Every once in a while the government, through the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) or some other minister tells us that there are programs being implemented to solve the unemployment problem. However, a measure like the one now before the House will only serve to increase unemployment and I think the government should drop this arrogance, this impression which it is giving to the whole population that he knows everything. Instead of that, he should follow the advice of opposition members who are somewhat closer to the people than those now running the country.
I therefore urge the government not only to postpone the tax, but to eliminate it immediately. By so doing it will have taken some concrete action toward creating

real employment opportunities because, with unemployment increasing at the present rate, it can be feared that the coming months hold in store a situation even more alarming than the one we now face.
On behalf of all moderate income citizens and workers of my riding, I therefore urge the government to assume its responsibilities and stop deceiving the population, to whom the assurance had been given that this 3 per cent surtax would be temporary. Let the government find ways and means of meeting its commitments and eliminate this tax within the shortest possible delay.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-225, now before us, is to amend the Income Tax Act and, in practice, its aim is to extend for one more year the 3 per cent surtax.
Hon. members will recall that when this surtax was imposed, it had been mentioned that it would be temporary only and that it would be recalled at the end of the year. And here we have its third renewal! It is the third time that Ministers of Finance ask the House to renew this so-called temporary tax. It is to be wondered whether it is the only possible and valid step in the circumstances. A temporary legislation has been turned into a permanent one.
It will be recalled that, when he brought down his supplementary budget on December 3, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) indicated that he intended to ask for an extension of this 3 per cent surtax on individual and corporation taxes.
Although this bill is not very elaborate, it includes, in my view, two important features which are in conflict with one another. On the one hand, the Minister of Finance would like to use taxation to stimulate the economy and, on the other hand, he proposes a measure that not only has the opposite effect, but will, to some extent, reduce the purchasing power of Canadian taxpayers.
I seriously wonder whether, in making this choice, the minister was motivated by political or economic reasons. If I have doubts it is because the bill under study includes two different decisions that lead us into completely opposite directions.
On the one hand, the minister proposes tax exemptions to stimulate investment and, on the other hand, he asks for the extension of the 3 per cent surtax. Those are two completely contradictory decisions. I wonder if in taking this decision the minister did not only consider the increase in tax revenue that this measure will bring in for the current year and which may reach $245 million. Obviously it is emphasized that tax exemptions of $25 million will be granted to companies and individuals that will increase their capital investments for the manufacturing processing of goods. But who will benefit by this measure besides big companies which invest continually and do not have to postpone projects for lack of available funds? How many taxpayers will really benefit by the increase in depreciation rate proposed in this bill? Very few. Only privileged people.

Moreover, the effect of this measure will be to increase further company reserves which are already too high in my estimation. I think that I can detect in the minister's decision his true choice which has a political rather than an economic character. By this decision, he enables large corporations to deduct $25 million from their income tax.
At a time when it would have been advisable to increase the total purchasing power of the people, the minister has made the wrong choice in extending the 3 per cent surtax thus depriving the people of $245 million.
I do not think that it is necessary to quote statistics on employment conditions in order to prove that the situation has not improved since December 3 last.
Even if the hon. minister declared recently that the number of unemployed should start declining after March, he certainly meant that the return of milder weather would be more efficient than the measures taken by the government to solve the unemployment problem.
To realize the situation one has only to check newspapers every day and one will learn about numerous layoffs in all sectors of industry. Nobody knows whether he or any member of his family will be unemployed tomorrow or next week.
There is no need to compare statistics or to play with figures to be able to say that things will be better tomorrow or worse in a week. We only know that too many people have lost their jobs and that unemployment has tremendous social and economic consequences.
I feel that the solution to an economic ill must be economic in nature and not political. To my mind, the minister chose a political solution.
The 3 per cent surtax we are asked to extend would remove an amount of money that should remain in the economic circuit, to sustain the demand for consumer goods. By sustaining it, at the same time we allow industries to continue producing, and service industries to pursue their economic activities, the result of which is to maintain or increase employment.
The taxpayer who lacks purchasing power buys less. The manufacturer produces less and, as a result of lower production, he lays off workers, and the cycle continues.
Such are the effects of the legislation proposed in Bill C-255 and other simliar ones. And one wonders how it is that results different from those anticipated are brought about. The present results, that is unemployment and underemployment, are not due to chance, but to a series of unconsidered decisions like that which is now proposed.
All taxes, whatever they are called, take away purchasing power from those who are hit by them. In particular, this tax will take $245 million from the taxpayers this year. That represents $245 million, at a time when it would have been necessary to inject supplementary capital in the economy in order to get it going again and to give new confidence to the people. With one hand, the minister collects a certain amount of money under the pretext that he must meet Treasury needs, and with the other, he allows an increase in the capital cost allowances on the purchase of equipment or production assets. Once

again, the citizen is forgotten to the benefit of companies. If this choice is not political, I wonder what it is!
We have been repeating for a long time, in this House, that the real problem is not at the production level, but at the consumer level. Our production system is without doubt able to supply all the goods needed for the welfare of the population, but the same cannot be said about the ability of the population to control production.
The minister still has time to withdraw Bill C-225 and to give up the extension of the 3 per cent surtax for another year.
I am sure that this decision would be well received by all Canadians. It would renew confidence in the economy of the country. We might see, during the following months, an economic recovery. Employment conditions would improve, and the minister would easily recover the $245 million, because he would not have to increase the government outlays for social welfare. Furthermore, the people returning to work would contribute to the tax receipts through income tax and various other taxes.
When the economic activity slows down, the government's tax receipts decrease also, and this is normal. The measure brought before the House by the Minister of Finance will contribute to increase taxes.
It seems to me we have had enough tax increases in Canada during the last ten years. The Canadian people are already overtaxed. From 1955 to 1965, tax increases at all government levels reached 41.4 per cent in Canada. There is no need to look far for an answer to the employment problem.
Whether we like it or not, all taxes are finally included in prices. That is why we must face constant and unreasonable price increases.
Who must pay for those price increases if not all consumers? Workers, people with a fixed income, low income groups are those who suffer the most from such increases, because every time prices go up, they have to do without some necessities.
Those who have an above average income are practically not affected by those increases, because they hold influential positions or operate at the management level. Those people often hold positions in manufacturing and trade. They can thus simply increase the price of their products or services. When they increase their prices, they improve the occasion sometimes by killing two birds with one stone, that is, by availing themselves of the latest price increases to increase their profits.
Who would not be tempted to do the same since our economical system is a jungle where the strongest makes its own law and is an absolute master? If the minister had taken some other course than to extend the 3 per cent surtax through Bill C-225, I would have been very surprised, because there is nothing he would not do to fight inflation.
For two years, the government deliberately restricted the Canadian economy and this led to a recession. Overnight the government, through the Prime Minister (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
March 4, 1971
Income Tax Act
Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), asserted that inflation had disappeared. However, during January, food prices in Quebec increased by about 2 per cent.
How is it that on December 3 they said that inflation had been checked and the aim was now to have unemployment disappear? It would have been more sensible to make sure what the genuine causes were before taking steps that led us to a dead end.
What about the fight against unemployment? It would have been better for them to keep silent, because since it was referred to, the number of unemployed increased by 200,000 and a considerable number of plants have closed their doors or reduced their business operations to such a level that they lose money every day.
This bill should be withdrawn immediately. This is hardly the time to impose new taxes. I believe that measures aiming at an injection of additional purchasing power should replace Bill C-225 now before the House. The measures taken should not slow down the economy but restart business.
Repeal of the 3 per cent surtax and of the 11 per cent tax on building materials was requested by all the representatives of the labour force and the expert spokesmen for the industrial, commercial and financial quarters.
Again I ask the Minister of Finance to withdraw his bill aimed at extending the duration of the 3 per cent surtax.

Mr. Speaker, some days the Commons chamber seems a little unreal. Outside in the country almost three quarters of a million Canadians are looking for work and experiencing the frustration of not being able to find employment. Inside this chamber, men of reason are gathered together to discuss a tax bill which is supposed to deal with this situation. Although the House can get angry and bitter on occasions, very little anger or bitterness is apparent today. In no way does the anger and bitterness felt outside the House permeate these walls.
We, as members of the opposition, appeal to the government to recognize what is happening and bring in measures which will be effective in reducing unemployment. Up to this moment, regretfully, we have not been successful. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is in his place most of the time. Perhaps he is behind the curtain now; I saw him only a little while ago. I am sure he says to himself: Oh, the opposition always talks, and no matter what we do they always complain. Thus, he lulls himself into a sense of complacency.
We are honoured today by the presence of a former minister of finance, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). So, in a way, there are two ministers of finance present in the House today while we debate one of the most crucial issues of our time. Yet, there is no response from across the way. They are quite convinced in their own minds that what they are doing is the best of all possible courses. They get very angry
when we on the opposition benches say the government has deliberately set out to create unemployment. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and other ministers, have said to the Canadian people on various occasions; how could anyone believe that we would deliberately create unemployment? They have worked out a little drill. They say they have done what they have done in order to avoid unemployment. In other words, they are throwing people out of work so that they will not be out of work. Well, they may be able to understand this reasoning but I find it difficult to do so. They say: If we had not done these things, conditions would have been worse. Of course, we have no way of knowing whether or not this is true.
The fact of the matter is that the government has made one of the most fantastic economic errors in the history of this country. They have failed to understand what is happening, and three quarters of a million Canadians are paying the price of their folly. The other day the Prime Minister had to admit before the Canadian Labour Congress, that had he known some of the things he knew later he might have brought in somewhat different policies. Perhaps anger is out of place here. We are reasonable men who come together to debate. After all, Parliament is a substitute for anger, a way of avoiding warfare and violence. This is the place where we can discuss these questions and, hopefully, come up with reasonable answers. Despite the fact that it has admitted making a mistake, the government puts forward no proposals designed to repair the damage, to get the economy going again. Hon. members opposite cannot make up for the hardship they have caused, the loss of human dignity. But at least they ought not to perpetuate it. They could take measures to get the economy going again. They have brought in measures which, they say, will move us in the right direction. Well, there is something to be said for not moving backward. Even a small step forward has to be appreciated. But we cannot be satisfied, faced with a problem of this magnitude and the suffering which is going on.
For a moment I want to leave recrimination aside. History will pass judgment as to whether the government deliberately created unemployment or not, or whether it simply goofed. The point is, what shall we do as a Parliament for the three quarters of a million Canadians who are out of work? The government points with pride to its export position, to the fact that we are exporting more than ever before. This is true, but what good is it when so many of our people are out of work? The fact that we are exporting at the present rate has raised the value of our dollar and hurt our manufacturing industry where most employment is concentrated. We have the worst record of employment in the western world, as well as the slowest growth. As a return for having created this situation, we have somewhat reduced the threat of inflation below the level it might have been.
To combat this unemployment, the government is proposing a measure to increase depreciation allowances from 100 to 115 per cent. I want to deal with that matter

March 4, 1971

in particular since it does cast a great deal of light on how the government views the situation and sees its priorities. What the government is really saying is that with an increase in depreciation allowances the road to recovery will be paved with increased profits for business, because that is really the effect of increasing depreciation allowances. There is the thought on the other side that if we are going to recover, slow though that recovery may be, the way to do so is to increase business profits and to show businessmen that more money is to be made. This, therefore, will stimulate capital expenditure, which in turn will stimulate the economy and employment will result. The point is there is no evidence that indicates that this in fact is going to happen, or that this particular kind of economic reasoning is any less disastrous than the economic policies that put us into this bind in the first place.
I should like to give the House some of my reasons for feeling as I do about this matter. First of all, if we look back to our periods of prosperity and examine the circumstances that motivated business, we will almost certainly find that the real stimulus to employment has always been increased purchasing power on the part of the consumer. Business is not going to expand even if you give business increased capital allowances. Some businesses are going to expand anyway, and it is a nice bonanza for them. We can kid ourselves later on that this expansion might not have taken place if we had not taken that step. The same can be said of the designated area program. Industry went into these areas, but we will never know whether industry went there because they were going there anyway or because of the giant hand-outs that we gave them.
As I say, there is no real evidence that these policies are effective. What we do know is that if people have needs that must be filled and have the means whereby they can pay for their needs, then businessmen will respond as they always have. After all, that is what business is all about. It is there to understand the demands made by society, and to provide the goods and services that arise as a result of those demands. Business cannot respond to those demands unless consumers have purchasing power.
It is for that reason that the members of this party, and I think this view is held also by all opposition parties, feel that it is purchasing power that has to be increased, not profits. My hon. friends to my left in the Creditistes have their own way of increasing purchasing power. I may not agree with that way, but they understand the problem, and in a way that the government does not. They know that the key to this problem lies in increasing the purchasing power of the people in one way or another. This is how you generate employment, and as business responds so you have business expansion.
There is no other way.

The other way that business responds, particularly in Canada, is in meeting needs that do not arise in our own country but in foreign lands. Unfortunately, too much business expansion has taken place in
Income Tax Act
this direction. For instance, much of the mining resource expansion takes place not because it is particularly good for Canada but because other countries desperately need our raw materials. This is a rather disastrous kind of development, one that is going to be accelerated and encouraged by the increased depreciation that is being proposed.
Let us look at some figures that appeared in the newspaper a few days ago. The Iron Ore Company of Canada is trying to justify the expenditure of $2 billion to develop an iron ore mine. They have pointed with pride to the fact that something like 9,000 jobs will be directly created. By a rough and ready rapid calculation this works out to $300,000 per job. It is true that additional jobs are created at the secondary and tertiary levels, but this is true of all industries, not just the mining industry. If it costs $300,000 to create one job, then how is this country ever going to be able to create sufficient employment for the estimated 200,000 people who enter the labour force every year? There is not that much money available to this country to create those jobs. I suggest the argument that we do not have enough capital in this country to provide jobs for our people is not true; not only do we not have enough capital in this country but no country in the world has enough capital to create jobs that cost $300,000 each. This is why we have to import capital.
Then the argument is made that this two billion dollars that is brought into the country results in purchases. Although a lot of this money does result in purchases in Canada, a lot of it is used to purchase foreign machinery. Much of it is used to make payments to foreign countries. With a rate of return on capital of only 10 per cent, we are talking about a figure of $200 million that has to be paid out to foreigners on an investment of $2 billion. This is a permanent drain on our resources resulting from capital that we should not have imported in the first place.
The difficulty is that the bill before the House is going to encourage this kind of development, a development that should have been discouraged a long time ago. The chief benefit being offered in this bill is an increase in capital investment. The mining industry is investing twice as much in capital development as the manufacturing industry. If we continue to pour money at this rate into industries which export raw materials from this country, then not only are we exporting jobs but we are exporting our future wealth.
Some economists might argue that the people who work for the Iron Ore Company of Canada earn higher wages than, let us say, people who work in the manufacturing industry in the city of Toronto. I understand the average wage with the Iron Ore Company is $9,000. What these economists do not say, of course, is that it costs a great deal more to live in that kind of environment and to provide the social services required in order to maintain production of raw materials.
If you listen to the economics purists, their conclusion is that Canada would be better off if we did not have to provide jobs for these 200,000 people coming into the labour force every year. In fact, 200,000 is a low estimate

manufacturing is increasing. What about the people in the provinces of Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan? The problems in those provinces are different. In many cases we have not been able to share the wealth generated in Ontario with other provinces, and this has created some resentment. If these provinces are to develop they must promote the exploitation of natural resources. There are a number of ways to change the situation. By using the Canada Development Corporation, we can increase industrial development through Crown corporations and partnerships in all parts of Canada.
We must support industry throughout Canada wherever it is possible to develop viable entities. The industrial revenues secured by Ontario should be distributed throughout the entire country in order that production is shared equally. We believe there should be an equitable distribution of the riches generated. The advantages of one province should be shared by other provinces. As long as the fruits of an industry are shared equally across the country, resentment will disappear.
My remarks have been sketchy and our time is limited during this debate. I have appreciated the opportunity to participate. Despite the calmness of our tone and the quietness of this Chamber, there is anger here and discontent. I think this Parliament should recognize that fact. It is still not too late for the government to withdraw this bill and substitute something more suitable to meet the crisis of this time.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-225. This afternoon I listened with interest to the speeches made both by the members of the Ralliement Creditiste and by the last speaker for the New Democratic Party. At the outset, I should say I am not really surprised at some of the statements made by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman). His party, consistently and persistently, has screamed at big, bad business. Obviously, some of the members of that party have not read Robert Tyres book which I believe is called "Douglas in Saskatchewan". This book would seem to indicate that there are none so righteous as reformed sinners.
I believe the bill before us should be referred to the committee as quickly as possible. If it can be referred to the committee this afternoon, there are a number of reasons why I believe that is exactly what should be done. I find little argument with the proposal of the minister and his parliamentary secretary that capital cost allowances should be extended into 1972. I intend to be one of those who welcomes such a proposal, particularly if it benefits business in any way.
I should like to see the bill go to committee because I believe business in this country should have an opportunity to appear before the committee to express either its objections or alternative proposals in respect of a capital cost allowance.

In extending the 115 per cent capital cost allowance into 1972, I think the government is being a little meagre. Normal industrial expansion or development takes place on a yearly basis, not merely because a particular corporation may want to take advantage of the 115 per cent capital cost allowance, so naturally this will more than offset any cost to the treasury as a result of this kind of concession. If the government really wants to assist business generally, and more particularly the construction business, it should immediately withdraw the tax on building materials. There is a chain reaction in respect of assistance to any business.
Some reference was made to the definition of businesses that will qualify under this program. Yesterday, as recorded at page 3924 of Hansard, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) said:
I might mention that the definition of a manufacturing or processing business and the description of assets qualifying for the supplementary allowance will be contained in regulations to be adopted soon after approval of the legislation.
Over the years, Mr. Speaker, you and I have watched situations in which days and indeed weeks have been spent on debating the merits and demerits of a given piece of legislation only to find in the end that the regulations which were drafted to put the bill into effect were so far removed from what Parliament intended initially that many Members of Parliament were left in complete bewilderment.
I say again that when this bill comes before the committee, I hope the minister will give committee members an opportunity to peruse the regulations. Then, not only the merits and demerits of the bill will be analyzed by the committee but also the regulations. As I said earlier, I agree wholeheartedly with the principle of assistance to business, but it appears to me the government seems to be giving a little with one hand and, in respect of future proposals, taking something away with the other. This kind of thing hurts. I would hope that some of the extreme proposals in the white paper, in so far as they affect the business community of Canada, would be withdrawn or given very serious consideration before being put into the form of legislation. I see no justification for the removal of protective tariffs on the importation of chemicals in the Kennedy Round negotiations of two years ago. I see no justification for compounding the problems of the chemical industry by pegging the Canadian dollar.
Perhaps at this point I might say something about the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin). To use a western term, the Minister "shafted" the wheat industry real well when he had the responsibility for that department. He has done an equally good job on the petro-chemical industry in Canada through what I think might be fairly called most inept negotiations in GATT. I think the net result of those negotiations was a loss for the Government of Canada and, indeed, for some of the industries in Canada. I wonder whether businessmen in this Chamber realize, notwithstanding what may be said

March 4, 1971
Income Tax Act
by our friends to the left, the penalties which have been imposed on business. In the years I have been in this Chamber, I have seen the implementation of Medicare and I have seen the implementation of the Canada Pension Plan. Unemployment insurance has been with us. The Workmen's Compensation Board is another penalty, as are unrealistic corporation taxes, local business taxes and real estate taxes on corporate property. Yet our friends to the left say the government is giving too much.
I say that I welcome the opportunity to invite the parliamentary secretary to bring this measure before a committee as quickly as possible to give the business community the opportunity to comment on the adequacy of the measure and to determine whether the business community feels this is the kind of legislation that will assist them in their growth and in the provision of jobs for which every member in this chamber is clamouring daily. No one denies that there is a serious unemployment problem, and I think all but a few of us in this chamber recognize that jobs can only be provided by the industrial community of this nation. I think this is the area on which the government must lean a little more heavily, so when the minister proposes his next budget we can see what we can do to provide a little incentive for business to grow. I suggest we give business a decent break and a chance to survive under our system, then perhaps some of those jobs that we are awaiting so anxiously from day to day will be forthcoming.
I say again that if a system provides an incentive for business to grow, business will not in any way restrict the number of people whom it will employ for the sake of greed or money. Expansion is in the mind of every manager in the country, and if the proper kind of tax incentives are given, the answer for which the minister is looking will be forthcoming. I think that one need only look at newspaper articles in the city of Edmonton to find that Chemcell has laid off 325 members of its staff this year as a result of action taken by this government no less than two years ago. I am not saying that the Kennedy round negotiations are directly responsible for cut backs in operations here or in Hardieville, Alberta, or indeed in Montreal or Brockville. There will be many more lay-offs in the petro-chemical industry in Canada unless some of the conditions negotiated some years ago are renegotiated to favour the Canadian industries, and some favourable concessions are made in the budget to come to allow these businesses to exist in Canada.
I think it is all well and good to talk about economic nationalism. May I remind members of this House that Canada would not be nearly the nation it is today if it were not for foreign investment which came into this country at the turn of the century. I can see nothing wrong with a Canadian tax structure to encourage investment from abroad. At the same time, I think that that kind of a tax structure should give Canadians an incentive to invest in Canadian natural resource development or industry along with foreign capital, provided
that we as a government can allow these people to operate under acceptable controls. A former Liberal member of this House of Commons, once a finance minister and now out of politics, the Hon. Walter Gordon, made some suggestions a few years ago with reference to a withdrawal tax. I was one of those who sat on the opposite side of the House but who rather favoured that kind of an arrangement. The hon. member for Waterloo said that foreign investment should be discouraged. If that is the case, he did not tell this chamber who in Canada would make the investments. Certainly, I would remind him again that he is not asking the government to make the investments in industry because he knows full well that a government once tried that and it failed miserably.
I want to comment only briefly on the surtax. I think that my attitude toward this part of the bill will be somewhat different. I think that extending this particular aspect of the bill is a retrograde step. The parliamentary secretary was not in the chamber on one famous night in February of 1968 when the government of that day proposed such a measure and was defeated by a vote of 84 to 82. I know that he was generous when he said, as recorded in Hansard of yesterday, that no surtax is paid by a single person whose income is below $2,743. I bet that there are not very many single people within the parliamentary secretary's social circle who earn under $2,743. He went on to say that neither is the surtax paid by a married man with two children whose income is below $4,343. That is pretty generous. What the parliamentary secretary is really saying is that we are not hurting very many people in this country, only about 98 per cent of those people who pay taxes. That is not very many. On the one hand, we are trying to encourage our people to buy Canada back and to invest in Canadian shares, stocks and bonds, and at the same time impose punitive tax, initially for one year. This tax was extended for another year, and now we are extending it for a third year. We say it is difficult to impose a tax, but it is much more difficult to remove it. This still applies.
I say that this bill should indeed go to committee, not because I think there will be many questions on the first part of the measure having to do with capital cost allowance. I think that will be generally and favourably accepted. But I think it should go to committee to get an expression of feeling for or against this measure, much like the treatment accorded the white paper proposals of last spring. Those people who are penalized, and will be penalized in the future should be given the opportunity to approve or object to this measure. At a time of high unemployment, the government should be looking at increasing personal exemptions rather than extending a punitive tax for which I think there is no reasonable justification.

that Bill S-10, An Act respecting La Societe des Artisans be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the main object of this bill, as set forth in the explanatory notes of Bill S-10, is, and I quote:
-to withdraw from this Society the attributes of a fraternal benefit society and to vest it with the rights and powers of a mutual life insurance company, while maintaining its representative form of government and allowing it to retain its power to promote social and educational activities.
The present bill would change the name of La Societe des Artisans. The proposed name will reflect the cooperative features of this institution.
I will recall a bit of history to help understand this bill. The Societe des Artisans, as I have just said, is a fraternal society for mutual support which started operations in 1876 under a provincial charter and has operated since 1917 under a federal charter. It is nearly 100 years old, and at first it wanted to pursue fraternal activities of social assistance and welfare for its members, with insurance as an accessory.
But as the Societe des Artisans now has more than 350,000 members and as its equity is in excess of $24 million, it seeks approval for this legislation now before us in order to deal effectively with the major and main activities of this corporation.
Under the terms of this request, it asks to be transformed into a mutual life insurance company while keeping its representative form of government.
This bill would also change its name. By becoming a mutual life insurance company, the Societe des Artisans, while remaining the property of its members, namely, the people insured and the contractants, will be empowered however to extend its activities to the whole
La Societe des Artisans
field of life insurance. Thus it will be possible for it to issue insurance policies on the lives of persons who are not within the family circles of its members, or still to generally re-insure life insurance contracts issued by other insurance institutions.
Furthermore, in becoming a mutual life insurance company, the Society will be subjected to the same controls as any other insurance undertaking (mutual or with capital outlay) under the authority of the Department of Insurance, and will reach the level of prestige that is common to institutions subjected to this kind of control.
On the other hand, the Society wishes to preserve the main objectives of its activities, namely mutual benefit, a co-operative nature, a specially elective formula, while modernizing its framework in line with the very great importance that the various forms of insurance have achieved within this Society.
The representative form of governing body which the Societe des Artisans now has, and wants to preserve, while changing into a mutual insurance company is defined in clauses 7 to 13 of the bill before us.
Within this administrative set-up, the areas where the Society is doing business are divided into local jurisdictions which in turn are brought together into regional jurisdictions.
Each member of the Society belongs to a local jurisdiction (generally that of his residence). The member may attend the meetings of that jurisdiction, may vote, be elected officer and delegate to the regional jurisdiction to which his local jurisdiction belongs.
Each regional jurisdiction is therefore composed of delegates from its local jurisdictions, and elects its own officers and delegates at the General Meeting.
The General Meeting, composed of delegates and of each regional jurisdiction (or their alternates) as well as existing directors and former presidents of the Society, is the highest legislative authority thereof.
The General Meeting is held at least once a year.
In addition to its legislative powers, it elects, every four years, the board of directors of the Society, as well as its president and vice-presidents.
According to the by-laws of the Society, each of its directors is elected to represent a regional jurisdiction on the Board of Directors.
The Society also wishes to change its name. The Society has for a very long time been very active in the co-operative movement.
By becoming a mutual life insurance company, while keeping at the same time its representative form of administration as previously described and the right to promote social and educational activities, the Society will keep all the characteristics of a co-operative.
It is this co-operative aspect that it wishes to underline in the new name: "The Artisans, Life Insurance Cooperative Society".
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the House will see fit to adopt this bill on second reading and that it will then

La Societe des Artisans
be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, which will be able to hear the officers of the Society as well as the Superintendant of Insurance who, by the way, has been heard by the Senate Committee and has said that he is in favour of this amendment to the Society and to the Act.
I thank the hon. members in advance for their cooperation.

Mr. Speaker, I read the bill a few minutes before entering the House, before five o'clock. In any case, I should like to put a few questions to the hon. member sponsoring the bill, asking him for clarification in the general interest.
First of all, I must say, and proudly, that I am a member of the Societe des Artisans and that the proposed change of name seems quite acceptable to me.
Investments are substantial enough in the Societe des Artisans to warrant the House giving the amendments put forward special consideration.
Now, will changing the name of the Society as well as some clauses authorizing it to enter into contracts with its members alter the character of existing contracts? Some contracts, for instance, are on the life of its members, while others do guarantee annuities to others.
This is what I want to know: Is the project now under study likely to alter in one way or other the contracts now in force?
Mr. Speaker, I believe that my question is in order because, normally we should get explanations enabling us to know whether this bill should be referred to the committee. We must know exactly the character of the proposed changes and the sponsor of the bill should be in a position to explain.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) asked the following question: What are the changes this new legislation will lead to in effective contracts in the insurance company? We must not forget that whenever a company operates on a fraternal society basis, since the main objective is not to sell insurance, insurance policies, the control, on the one hand, and the requirements on the part of the Superintendent of Insurance on the other hand, are greater, but this is due to the flexibility of operations in the fraternal society and to the risks that may to a certain extent be involved.
This means that a fraternal society may in the course of its operations, although it has never been done, change the contract and ask, for instance, that an additional sum be paid because the operating costs seem greater or the death rate exceeds the estimates, etc.
Therefore, whenever the society operates as a mutual company, it is impossible then to change the contracts and to call for new payments on premiums. And this becomes firm in that way.
I think those references do not minimize the present operations of La Societe des Artisans, because they have never changed the premiums during the run of a contract. But it was possible under the statute of a fraternal society while now, and because the society wants it, it is operating more on the basis of an insurance corporation and thus cannot change in any way the premium and the contracts.
It is obvious that all the policies being sold at the present time are not changed in any way and security is thus increased.
I should like to avail myself of this opportunity also to thank the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Ricard) for his kind words and of his reference to the success of one of our companies, of which we are rightly proud.
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate you on your recovery. We are happy to see you in the Chair again and we wish you a long stay among us.

I am informed by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources that correspondence received from uranium-producing and exploration companies contains information specifically requested by the government and given with the assurance that it would be treated as confidential. In view of this, I trust the hon. member will agree to withdraw his motion.
As recorded at page 868 of Hansard, I said that was not acceptable and the motion was transferred for debate. I did not ask for this information merely because I wanted the government to reveal information which is confidential. I think all hon. members of the House recognize that some correspondence between the government and other parties must be confidential. private papers reflecting correspondence between the government and the uranium industry. In this case, the documents refer particularly to the position of Denison Mines and the government of Canada in light of Mr. Roman's announcement that he intended to sell his company to interests outside Canada.
The confidential nature of such documents is something which has to be established over a period of years. We cannot let it be destroyed unilaterally by one of the parties concerned simply because a motion has been put down requesting us to make those documents available. I am sure there is information contained in these documents which would benefit neither the government nor the individuals concerned. I need hardly point out that the interests of the shareholders of the company could be affected by such a disclosure.
We all remember the great excitement in the fifties when prospectors and others moved across the length and breadth of Canada searching for uranium deposits. We recall the establishment of such communities as Elliot Lake and Uranium City. Elliot Lake grew from being a spot in the bush to a modern, well equipped town. Then, as a result of a decision in the United States, the industry entered a period of decline. Mines were closed down and towns like Uranium City were seriously affected. We were unable to sell our product-though not the ore itself-in the markets of the world.
Sales by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited have been disappointing, to say the least. I remind hon. members that many years ago Canada decided that its approach to the use of atomic power was through heavy water process. Other countries took a different approach. Almost alone in the world, Canada depended on heavy water. Consequently, we found we were unable to convince other nations that this was the best way of developing nuclear energy.
Having gone through these ups and downs, the industry nevertheless looks forward to a bright future. This is what has been said for some time. Most of us wonder if that day will ever come. Nevertheless, we have kept a uranium industry in Canada by means of a combination of stockpiling on the part of the government and occasional sales of uranium ores to other countries, under certain restrictions. We have insisted on certain safeguards, specifying that whatever uranium we sold should not be used for military purposes. Canada has been a leader in the sale of uranium for peaceful purposes. On at least one occasion a major sale was not consummated simply because the other country concerned was unable or unwilling to guarantee that the product would be used for peaceful purposes and not for the manufacture of nuclear weapons.
As I say, we have retained the basis of an industry which will mean much to us in the future. There are still large deposits of uranium ore under the ground and many mining companies are anxious to get on with the work of developing their ore bodies whenever the market permits. In the meantime, the government determined that it was not in the national interest to permit the sale of a major company in this country to a foreign concern.

Having taken that approach, since that time there has been a period of negotiation and discussion between the government and the company concerned, much of which has been on a confidential basis and has been, I assume, an expression of ideas and opinions on the part of both. To make this kind of information available to the public through this House would not, I think, be in the best interests of the company or of the people of Canada.
To return to my original point, which was that confidence must be established, be it in the uranium industry or in any other industry, between government and the private sector, the principle involved is similar to the case where a man files an income tax return knowing that the return will not be distributed to other government agencies but will be kept within the revenue department. Similarly, a man who fills out a census form for the decennial census knows that the information he gives will be for the use of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, and under penalty of fine or imprisonment the employees of DBS are required to ensure confidentiality of the information. The same principle applies in these particular cases as to all other cases involving such negotiations between government and the private sector.

The head of a family who earns $4,000 a year receives the equivalent of welfare. And if people on welfare had to pay taxes, it would be of the utmost ridicule. When somebody with an income below $5,000 is taxed, the essential needs of a family are thus taxed. And even though the government is very strong presently, owing to its majority, I feel it is not a good enough reason for it to take the last nickel away from the Canadian people.
When we compare in the 1971-72 budget the amount of $558,300,000 paid in respect of family allowances to the amount of $1,994,685,000 for servicing the debt, we find ample reason to convince us that the present government does not at all reflect the image of the democratic government which had been expected following the coming to power of the Liberal party. By its action, the present government is in the process of proving that it does not at all administer the country according to the wishes of the people.
The minister who is supposed to sponsor this bill is not alone responsible for this state of affairs, as there is above the governments an anonymous body which includes very influential people who are being waited on by the old political parties. Whatever the color of the government, blue or red, it is always the same administration dictated by senior officials whose function is to execute the will of high financiers. Crises of all kinds follow one another. There are words to categorize them, they are even given names as for hurricanes: the monetary crisis, the October crisis, the unemployment crisis, the union crisis. It is easy enough to catalogue all those crises but when it comes to finding means to prevent them, nothing is done. The government is sustaining constant publicity about the poor; the number of poor people increases but there is no mention of change of any kind.
Mr. Speaker, precisely because I did not come here to protect any trust, because I am primarily concerned about the welfare of my constituents, I take the liberty of moving the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Shelford (Mr. Rondeau):
That the main motion be amended by deleting the word "now" and adding the words "in six months from today" at the end of the question.

Mr. Speaker, it is easy to settle immediate problems with instant stop-gaps applicable at any time. The government, which was supposed to establish the just society, lost no time, right after taking office, in raising taxes through a 3 per cent surtax.
The new administration, under the spell of "Trudeau-mania", had already raised taxes by 2 per cent, affixing to the new tax the pretentious name of social development.
Ironically enough, never has Canada known such gloomy years! Unemployment, social deterioration and anarchy seemed to be the reaction to this half-concealed arrogance. The Canadian citizen is more and more aware of the fact that constant imposition of new taxes and surtaxes will fatally lead to a point of no return, where anarchy and dictatorship are bound to take over.
Income Tax Act
Too often, and this should never have been tolerated, temporary schemes end up by being permanent. This illustrates the principle: let us create a precedent, let us enact a temporary legislation; in any case, it will become permanent.
We, particularly in Quebec, in the past, have greatly suffered the ill effects of such provisional agreements that later on became permanent. How many essential rights Quebec has lost temporarily and which are the cause of the accute constitutional conflicts we are experiencing today! How many promises of a return to normal as soon as the dangerous situation was controlled! In a word, Mr. Speaker, how many misrepresentations, at least at the intellectual level, aimed at improverishing the Canadian taxpayer to a greater extent!
Perhaps we could not talk this way if we had no other solutions to put forward than those constant tax increases. My colleagues had the opportunity to analyse scientifically and refute systematically the claims of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson).
Allow me to emphasize, in my own way, the disadvantages of this obsolete economic system which requires the whole population to follow the ups and downs of a staggering economy controlled by the whims of high finance. If at least the government, through its action, managed to restore some order within the economy, if it succeeded in improving everybody's welfare, and if finally, it succeeded in balancing once and for all the country's finances, we would not insist so much that this bill be withdrawn. But God knows that everybody is lost in this fiscal jungle. The government is groping its way day by day. Money is so scarce: it does not matter whether this is the result of bad administration or of a bad system, it keeps on levying more taxes to solve whatever problem arises.
And yet the means we are suggesting should at least be tried out. Let us stop empoverishing everybody by this dreadful bleeding from interest scattered to all winds, the North-South wind being the most efficient.
Why persist in requesting from senior bankers permission to issue social credit? Why reimburse two, three, four and even five times the capital amount? Why thus spoil the genuine power, that of the people, the monetary power that the people himself could exercise through his bank, the Bank of Canada?
Why not agree to interest-free loans? Why not reduce by all means available the tax burden and avoid all extravagance?
Mr. Speaker, we would very much like the government to succeed in making our economy healthier. We would like to help them do it. With all our heart we would like to be able to relax in this vast country of ours whose untold riches do not sufficiently contribute to the welfare of each and every one of us. We would so much like every Canadian to feel really responsible and to be able, having acquired his full development at all points of view, to contribute to international development, to inter-
